implementation_notes: C++ mud is usually a wide header that every .cpp includes, plus a namespace of free functions and extern globals that act as the system's registry. The C++-specific diagnostic is the compile-time one: if changing a widely-included header rebuilds the whole project, that is a measurable statement about coupling that no architecture diagram will dispute. Consolidation is genuinely cheap here — namespaces, `inline` variables in headers (C++17) instead of extern globals, and the PIMPL idiom for reducing the include graph — which makes it a good target language for a first consolidation pass.
idiom_name: one translation unit with a global namespace containing the system
pitfalls: A header defining inline variables (or non-inline functions) still exposes everything it declares to every includer; the include graph is the coupling.
`using namespace` in a header turns the mud into a global namespace problem with an added step.
Templates and inline functions in a common header amplify the blast radius of any change to that header.
